utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We continue this morning with the evidence of Mr. Gagic, who will be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, who has transmogrified into Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue with cross-examination by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning continues to apply to your evidence throughout. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gagic. I just wanted to clarify a couple of questions about your background. Yesterday you told us that you started working at the ministry headquarters in 1996 and that after that you worked on crime prevention with the crime prevention police. You said: "At the outset I dealt with property-related crime and juvenile delinquents and between 2002 and my retirement I dealt with murder." So that sounds like you worked on property crimes and juvenile delinquents between 1996 and 2002, but from what I read in your 65 ter and what I think you said later, I got the impression that you had started working on sex crimes and murder crimes sooner than that. Can you help me out. Can you tell us exactly when you worked on which types of crimes?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you probably didn't get the right picture. I started working with the Ministry of the Interior back in 1980. As for the ministry HQ, the Ministry of the Interior I mean, as an executive body of the police I started working there in 1996. So between 1980 and 1996 I first dealt with property-related crime and juvenile delinquency up until sometime around 1991. As of 1991 I started working with the Belgrade SUP where I had first started working in the ministry, one of its organizational units, it was sometime late in 1991 and 1992. I worked murder and sex-related criminal offences. And then I switched to the ministry, the seat of the ministry, and then between 1996 and 2004 I was dealing again with murder, homicide, and sex offences. I was the chief of that particular department. Between 2004 and my retirement I worked as chief of the department for discovering war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand now. You mentioned meetings at the MUP staff facility, and I'm talking about 1999. I'd like to start by looking at Exhibit P1996. I think you were shown part of this document yesterday. Now, I've got a hard copy I can have the usher hand you. This is from a meeting on the 7th of May, 1999, in Pristina, and on the first page you'll see that along with those attending were your boss, Major-General Dragan Ilic and also Vladimir Aleksic from the forensic centre, forensic investigation centre and Sinisa Spanovic from the head of the department in the UKP. What was -- can you explain to me, what was your position in relation to those other two gentlemen, Aleksic and Spanovic? Were you sort of equals, were you on the same level with them?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksic was the head of department, the criminal forensic centre is a department. He outranked me. He was a head of department, and Sinisa Spanovic was a head of section. We were at the same level. There was no subordination between us because we did completely jobs in terms of his function, Aleksic was above me and Sinisa Spanovic was at the same level, but in terms of the nature of our respective jobs, we were quite independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was Spanovic's job, what was his department or section? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spanovic was head of the search department, the sort of thing that his sector did was they looked for suspects and perpetrators. Every time there was a police search or a judicial search, perpetrators, suspects and also unidentified perpetrators, those were the people -- the groups of people they tried to track down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if it's necessary to note this, but there's something missing from the transcript, a complete answer, but no doubt that will be rectified later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could go to I think it's on page 8 of the B/C/S hard copy you have and for those of us following in English it's page 9. There should be a reference there, sir, to the meeting being given or the floor being given to General Ilic to speak and then it talks about the things he talked about. Do you find that where General Ilic is speaking?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw that. I didn't attend the meeting myself, but I've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I realize you didn't attend this meeting and I have a couple of questions about that. First of all, why weren't you at this meeting? It seems like some of the topics that are being discussed by General Ilic here are things that would relate to your particular job. Were you aware of this meeting and just unable to attend or were you told it wasn't necessary? Why weren't you there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend this meeting although I knew that the meeting would be held simply because I was busy elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what you were doing on the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific, but I think that was the day I went to Glogovac. I mentioned Hasan Corbic who was a military officer. I think that was the date. Other than that at the time this meeting was held and at the time generally speaking I was working full tilt on lists with statistical information because this was a priority task that I was dealing with at the time and they had to be completed in no time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You see the first thing that General Ilic mentions, that there was a meeting held on the 5th of May, 1999, at the staff in Pristina with the chiefs of SUP UKP at which precise task and instructions were given on how the work of crime investigation police should proceed, and I think you told us before you didn't attend that meeting either on the 5th of May, right? I'm sorry, I'm not sure they were able to pick up your answer. Would you say it again out loud?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I hadn't attended the previous meeting either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again that one sounds like maybe it's even more specifically related to your kind of work, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were high-ranking officers present at the meeting and that was quite sufficient, I mean their presence. And we could dish it out among ourselves. We talked, they told me who had attended the meeting, but none of this was necessary because there were already three high-ranking police officers at the meeting. It wouldn't have been a good thing if it ended up seeming as though there were more of us from the police at the meeting than the other guys. It wasn't necessary for too many people to get involved, although I can go back and at least I can read the tasks, and I can also consult with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So at the meeting on the 5th was that also General Ilic, Mr. Aleksic and Mr. Spanovic, you know that those three attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know all three of them were at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall where you were on the 5th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I abide by my previous answer. I was hard at work on introducing those statistical lists I was gathering modules and forms, and my work focused on that sort of thing over those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But at the time back in May 1999 you were aware of these meetings and what was being discussed at them, were you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next thing that General Ilic mentions, the tasks were clearly defined and then it goes on to say: "But there has not been sufficient efficiency when pursuing all types of criminals in the Kosovo-Metohija area." Do you know what types of criminals were being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All different types of crime or criminals. The conditions were difficult, it was difficult to investigate and take any steps. The ability at the time was down to a bare minimum. It was very difficult to prosecute effectively, it was difficult to achieve anything resembling peacetime conditions. The principal task was for those working on crime prevention to be motivated in some way. There had to be permanent pressure, there had to be meetings and dispatches containing instructions in order to get the best of the work and the chief -- the best result possible. In actual fact, the results we saw across there just didn't please us not those achieved anywhere, but this was largely due to the difficult conditions that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Continue on to the second point after that, if you will, if and for those in English we have to go to the top of page 10. It mentions: "A meeting was held with VJ top officials, at which it was agreed that measures were being applied, but they were not sufficient at the moment." Did you know about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you move on three points down, my English translation says: "A plan of restoring territory has been compiled and distributed to all the SUP UKP ..." Do you know what that plan of restoring territory was?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that plan, I'm not even sure if it existed. There was a dispatch containing a set of instructions or a letter that was drafted at more or less the same time and it talked about exactly all the same things that we have been talking about, stepping up of activity and crime prevention, that sort of thing. There is a document talking about that, there is a reference there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a question. Your answer was translated as: "I never saw that plan, I'm not even sure if it existed." This is General Ilic speaking at the meeting. Do you have any doubt that there was a plan, he said: "The plan has been compiled and distributed ..." I understand you say you never saw it, but do you have any reason to doubt General Ilic when he said that at this meeting? Mr. Sainovic was at this meeting, General Stevanovic was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt that General Ilic said that at the meeting, but I'm not sure if he meant what you think he meant, this being a plan with detailed instructions on what to do or was this just a generic set of instructions saying that on-site investigations should continue to be carried out, that crimes should be uncovered, perpetrators identified, and that they should get on with that. I know that there is a document like that, but it's certainly not "asanacija" plan as reflected in this document. I think it might be worded differently and probably also written differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the B/C/S does it say "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Saniranje."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said just now that you think that this -- you said: "I'm not sure if he meant what you meant," meaning me, "this being a plan with detailed instructions -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think he has the document in front of him, but it doesn't say, "asaniranja" but "saniranje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was the spelling we were given yesterday. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if you read that whole sentence it says: "A plan of restoring territory has been compiled and distributed to all the SUP UKP which specifies and clearly defines assignments." That sounds like more than just a generic set of instructions, it specifies and clearly defines assignments, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this document seems to indicate, but I've never seen the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it existed because even if I didn't come across it at the time I probably would have seen it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, why in the world were General Ilic be referring to a non-existent plan at this meeting attended by the deputy prime minister and General Stevanovic? That doesn't make any sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right. It appears here that he's misinforming the state leaders, and this is certainly not something that General Ilic was normally in the habit of doing. It wasn't typical of him, that's why I have to say this. I'm afraid that there's a gap between what he said and what was recorded in the transcript, there is a discrepancy, because what a transcript normally reflects or minutes of a meeting is normally an abridged version of what was actually said and he was probably saying that this was about instructions, about what to do whenever human remains were found and whether any procedure applied on such occasion was perfectly in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I must object to the way these questions are being asked. All right, maybe Sainovic has no place in this context, but it's certainly out of the question that his name should be taken in a way that is untruthful based on all of the evidence that we have seen so far, he was there at the beginning and then he left. General Ilic talks about all, all of the witnesses so far, and Sainovic is not there, no exception. Sainovic is being used here as some sort of a catch word and I simply have to oppose it. This is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document reflects that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic took part in the meeting, and my point is this claim that General Ilic is talking about a non-existent plan makes less sense to me if he's speaking at a meeting where big shots, like the deputy prime minister, is attending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does it show the part he played?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 1, Your Honour, under the minutes it says the deputy prime minister, Nikola Sainovic, took part in the meeting. So I'm assuming he's present when General Ilic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there is a clear suggestion in what Mr. Lukic says that he has made a speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, he does speak at page 2 of the English, Your Honour, at some length, page 2 to 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fila, this is a matter for re-examination. There is foundation for the questions. If you want to challenge this you'll be given an opportunity if it appears that you would otherwise be prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I won't be taking that opportunity because the witness said he wasn't at the meeting at all, so therefore I probably can't ask him for how long Sainovic was at that meeting for because the witness wasn't there. All I'm saying is the Prosecutor heard it right. All of the witnesses heard mentioned in this transcript and there's at least seven of them I think have been heard so far, so that Sainovic gave a speech and left. Therefore, he couldn't possibly have been at the meeting at the time General Ilic took the floor. So I'm looking for a foundation for this question and what I'm actually suggesting is this is not true because everybody so far has been saying the same thing. Sainovic spoke and he left. He came, he spoke, he left, and all of the witnesses heard so far have been saying the same thing. That's what I'm saying. I don't think the witness could help us see the way, by the way but Mr. Hannis knows this full well, and if I can put it that way I think he's doing it deliberately, and I'm not re-examining if that's what your wondering about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you've said is a matter for submission, it's a matter for us to decide which parts of the evidence we accept, and that we will do in due course, but there's nothing improper about the question being put the way it was. We note that you claim, and you're right, that the question is just as valid without any reference to the individual personalities. The real issue here is whether the statement made is a misleading one or an accurate one and it doesn't really matter who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, that's fine, the question is fine. But Mr. Hannis has a copy of these minutes in his hands and you can tell that Mr. Lukic thanks Sainovic. Sainovic is on his way out, and it isn't before such time that Ilic actually takes the floor. Let's just try to be a bit more honest and not insinuate anything. You can tell that General Lukic is thanking Sainovic. Yeah, yeah, yeah, it's there. If you go back to the document you'll see it right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our position remains the same. There's nothing wrong with your question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have to indicate I'm not being dishonest. I don't see an indication here that he left. I see that General Lukic thanked him for his remarks but it doesn't say he then left, so I resent the implication that I'm being dishonest with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Fila's comment is based on the oral evidence of other witnesses that we've heard so far, but however I agree with you that there's no basis for suggesting that your conduct is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's important, Mr. Fila, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Moving down from where we were, Mr. Gagic, I think it's one, two, three, four, five bullet points down there's a reference to Article 218. Can you tell us very briefly what Article 218 refers to.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you off the bat. I think it's probably something from the Law on Criminal Procedure, but I wouldn't know those off the cuff. I always get a copy of whichever law it is that I'm supposed to be a applying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, here it says specifically: "With regard to conduct in accordance with Article 218, a suspect must be questioned during the investigation and all the measures and tasks that are involved must be included ..." Is this Article 218 something that's more applicable to a -- an investigative judge or a prosecutor than it would be to you doing the kind of work you did or do you know?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I know, but 218, I can't just quote the article off the top of my head or explain it and I don't remember which particular article that was because you know there are quite many of those. But what's being discussed here is in actual fact that instead of the procedure that you used to apply when interviewing witnesses -- because we're not interrogating witnesses, we interview them. A statement was taken and an official note drawn up as part of the procedure that applied. In the meantime there was a module that was drawn up to contain any witness's or suspect's personal details first of all, so that was what page 1 of each of those modules was about. It was about the personal details of whoever is being interviewed and the rest was freestyle you might say. So the module was changed to some extent but the essence remained the same. The module that was introduced now began to be used on the eve of the air-strikes, and I think that's what Dragan Ilic was talking about. He was talking about this, that modules should be used as envisaged in Article 218, those modules were being used, they were pre-printed, so to speak, and he was saying not to use the free-style approach that the previous procedure had envisaged for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned yesterday that "asanacija" was a new term for you when you heard it in, what, Kosovo in 1999? Was that the first time you heard the term?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for "asanacija," it's something that I heard before as a term but not in a military sense. I even heard the term being used in medicine, meaning that somebody was being taken care of, was being assisted in the medical way, he was being helped. And "asanacija" should be exactly the opposite, but I never heard it as a military term. I did hear the term in other areas of life. I maybe used it myself occasionally maybe to mean -- to signify a totally different kind of activity, and that's precisely why I started looking into this, because I refused to be directly or indirectly involved in something that I didn't even though the meaning of, but then I came across this term, "asanacija" [as interpreted] of the battle-field and that caused an entirely different reaction in me and simply led me to familiarize myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 13, line 7, witness said: "I even heard the term," and the term actually is missing, it is "saniranje," without a and it's the term which he explained later on before explaining "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in conjunction with the military use of this term, when did you first become aware of it, was that you heard somebody say it or you saw it in a document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be too long a story if I were to tell you how I first came across this. This was totally informal, totally unofficial. Actually, I first heard the term twice informally, unofficially, then I leafed through the military encyclopedia and then I realized that it had to do with dealing with the possibilities of hazardous effects on person's health --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's try and keep it short if we can. You said you first heard it twice informally. Can you tell us when and where that was and who you heard it from?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I wanted to avoid, this long story. The first time I heard this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Gagic, that doesn't need a long story. You've been asked who told you, who mentioned it to you, and what were the circumstances, in other words, when and where. That's three words that you give, the name, the place, and the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. I cannot respond in three words. The courier of a military officer was looking for me at the Forensic Medicine Institute in Pristina, he was asking for Dr. Galic for "asanation" while I was working on Pusto Selo, so the story continues. The second time I heard about it was when I went as a private person to visit a friend of mine from the army and the duty officer who was supposed to announce my arrival said that this officer had gone away to deal with "asanacija." So it was completely new to me, and then I realized that really I had to deal with it and find out what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the rest of your answer about that yesterday you said you also had an occasion to see a document, an order, in the "naredba" that had been issued by the army in relation to "asanacija." Can you tell me what that document was and when and where you saw it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document I saw at the Pristina SUP at the then-head of the crime police's office because actually I came there to ask him whether he knew what this word meant in our war conditions. He showed me this order, I read the order, although it was confidential but I am an authorised official so I could familiarize myself with its content. That is to say that I read it, and I saw that both procedures were in line with the Law on Criminal Procedure but military and civilian authorities act in a significantly different way. We have a system whereby the executive and the judiciary is completely separated, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. That's not answering the question. Approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was say between the 25th of April and the 1st of May, while I was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall from whom the document or order came? You say it was issued by the army, but do you recall a unit or an individual from whom it came?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the command, the military command, that had issued it I think but I really cannot assert this, that the signature is that of General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that document since that date in late April or around the 1st of May, 1999? Did you see it while preparing for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the document because I was working on the KiM dossier in terms of armed conflicts in Kosovo, so I had occasion then to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1999 or 1998, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I took him to be referring to 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 25th of April and the 1st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did you do work on the KiM dossier, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I worked on that sometime from 2001 when this dossier was first being established, at least my line of work, missing persons, and all the way up until I retired. It's not that that was my basic task, but I did participate in the establishment of this dossier by providing documents and by analysing documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked by Mr. Lukic if you'd heard anything about a proposal to set up a joint commission between the VJ and the police, and I think this was in connection with dead bodies in Kosovo and you said, No, you heard no such thing. And then you were asked a hypothetical question by Mr. Lukic. He said: "Say, for example, a joint committee of the VJ and the police the MUP was set up, could it possibly take over the powers of the investigating judge of all the other bodies normally involved in a procedure like this?" And you said: "First of all, under the law no such committee could be established and secondly it would require several hundred people." You're not a lawyer, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about a joint committee between the MUP and the VJ, solely for the purpose of establishing which of those two entities was in an area at the time that dead bodies were found, there would be no legal bar to setting up that kind of joint committee would there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but that's my question to you. There -- this is a different question --

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's the question. I thought -- well, no, as I said during the previous examination, such a body could be established only for following a particular subject matter from the point of view of analysis but not functionally. This body -- well, it depends on how you treat it, I mean whether it would have to do with "saniranje" or "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but if the only purpose is trying to determine which of the two entities the army or the MUP were carrying out operations or actions in a particular area at the time those dead bodies became dead bodies instead of living human beings, there is nothing in the law that would prevent setting up a joint commission or a joint committee to sort that out between the MUP and the VJ, there's no reason they couldn't do that, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be no bar to establishing such a commission, but there was no need to establish such a commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that during your time in Kosovo that you didn't have any responsibility toward General Lukic as the head of the MUP staff nor towards any other member of that staff, no responsibility whatsoever is what you said. You went on to say: "The only commitment that I did have in my own line of work was to report to whichever official was in charge of crime." So could you tell us, who would be the official "in charge of crime"? Is that somebody in each of the respective SUPs? Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say that I had to report to any person that was in Kosovo and Metohija. Perhaps a mistake was made in the transcript. I did not report to anyone; I would inform the person who was in charge of crime about my own movement in Kosovo and Metohija for a simple reason, that it is known that I am in Kosovo and Metohija for my sake and for the sake of the other people involved. That is to say if I go out into the field and I do not come back, if I do not get to an appropriate secretariat that means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Blagojevic, who worked on crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, he worked in the MUP staff. You're being asked who your superior was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My superior in Kosovo was no one whatsoever. Dragan -- General Dragan Ilic in terms of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were a free spirit, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who were you answerable to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To General Ilic and his assistant or the head of the department, it depends on who I was given this task by. I was responsible to those who sent me there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that later on you became a member of the MUP staff, and I think we saw that in Exhibit P1811 yesterday where you were appointed a member of the MUP staff. You know you were recommended by General Lukic to become a member of the staff, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lukic proposed me because work is done on the basis of proposals rather than recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one of the questions that we've had early in this case was whether or not General Lukic as head of the staff had any ability to affect appointments. I would like to show you Exhibit 6D366, if I could. I don't know if you will have seen this before or not, Mr. Gagic. Do you recall having seen it? It's dated the 28th of May, 1999, from General Lukic to the Ministry of the Interior to -- actually to General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't had an opportunity to see this document, but I did have an opportunity to see the decision on the establishment of the staff that stemmed from this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And isn't it correct that of the ten people proposed here by General Lukic to make up the staff effective 1 June 1999 indeed were all named by Minister Stojiljkovic in that order that you saw the other day in Exhibit P1811? Everybody that General Lukic proposed was named to the staff by Minister Stojiljkovic, right? Do you need to see the other exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I may have a wrong document in front of me, but here I see the proposal for termination of tenure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, read the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see anybody proposed, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you have the same as --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it help you, Mr. Gagic, to see P1811 side by side with that one so you can check?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no need for that. What I see here at the same time is whose engagement is being terminated and who was being proposed for the new staff. I think that this is a technical procedure in actual fact. This is prescribed by internal regulations of the Ministry of the Interior. Who it is that makes proposals, who makes nominations or appointments, and who sends people to different places, and of course consultations take place before that among the different lines of work because this was probably preceded either by a document or an oral agreement with -- between General Lukic and the heads of the lines of work. In my particular case it was General Ilic and he probably proposed me, my name. However, in order not to have six different types of proposals, then there are these oral consultations or perhaps consultations in writing and then General Lukic sends a proposal in writing --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you there. You're going well beyond my question. My question was just: Isn't it correct that the ten people named here and proposed by General Lukic indeed were named in the decision by Minister Stojiljkovic to become part of the new staff effective at the beginning of June 1999, right? All of General Lukic's proposals were accepted and followed, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, because that had been agreed upon beforehand, before this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you know that? Did you sit in those meetings with General Lukic and Minister Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was asked by my chief, General Ilic, to come and see him and he asked me whether I could and wanted to be a member of the staff as of the 1st, because the staff was being changed and this kind of a proposal was supposed to be sent to General Ilic. I agreed with that. Now, whether Dragan Ilic informed Lukic orally or in writing, and then I don't know. But at any rate I had been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't know what the situation was with the other nine people, do you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite identical. I state with full responsibility that General Lukic did not know more than half of these people so he couldn't have made proposals concerning them. They were proposed to him and then he just made the proposals formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're saying he didn't know half these people? Can you tell me which half he didn't know?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that General Lukic knew Vojislav Gucic, I'm not sure that General Lukic new Dragan Lukic, I'm not sure that he knew Petar Bogdanovic -- or actually, some of these people were from the old composition of the staff so he knew them from there but probably he hadn't known them before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So he's only known them for a year, right, like Dr. Krdzic, who had been on the staff for the previous year?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you about the principle involved. He knew them if they were old members of the staff; as for new members of the staff that were proposed by his organizational units, very often he would not know them and he would only meet them once they came to the staff. That is to say it wasn't General Lukic's free choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you talk to General Lukic about that, whether it was his free choice or not, you didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Look at number 2, Lieutenant-Colonel Arsenijevic, he had been part of the staff since 3 April 1999, so General Lukic must have known him for at least those seven or eight weeks, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is being written here is that his assignment is being terminated, Goran Radosavljevic, of course he knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about Goran Radosavljevic, I'm asking you about number 2, Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Arsenijevic, already part of the staff since 3 April 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on the staff and General Lukic, of course, knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of course he knew Major Bogdanovic, which is not what you told us just a little bit ago, because he had been on the staff since the 8th of April, 1999, that's what it says here?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. What I'm claiming is the people who were sent to the staff for the first time, usually the head of the staff personally does not know these people visually either. Later on he gets to know them. I'm sure that General Lukic never saw Tomislav Blagojevic, my predecessor, who was sent from Krusevac to the staff and his first encounter with him was in the month of February when he was sent to the staff. So I'm talking about that principle. It does not necessarily mean that these people that General Lukic proposed are General Lukic's choice. They are the choice of the heads of the organizational units, and consultations take place before Lukic actually makes the proposal. It is in that context that I said this, that indeed quite a few of these employees were -- well, there. But if you take the new staff for the AP KiM that was established on the 15th of July after the bombing, I am sure that once --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. I'm not interested in that. That's not what my question was about. You did tell us that you didn't think that he knew Colonel Bogdanovic and here it states that Colonel Bogdanovic had already been a member of the staff since the 8th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He backed off of that very quickly, Mr. Hannis, and qualified it in exactly that way when the answer was given. The point the witness is making is that there's a system that operates that you're not familiar with. Whether it was actually operating in this case is undoubtedly the issue that you're pursuing. But he is not the first witness to tell us all these things are stitched up before the proposal is actually made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're telling us that during the course of year that General Lukic would not know, would not have opportunity to see face-to-face the members of the MUP staff of which he was the head? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that General Lukic did not have to know a member of the staff if he was being changed or being re-assigned unless in his previous activities he had worked in his line of work and therefore they met at work, not knew them. That is to say it wasn't his initiative but consultations took place with the heads of the organizational units, and they know better who should be sent in terms of the work that had to be done, they know better than anything General Lukic could propose on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And so I take it then you're saying that when Minister Stojiljkovic makes the final decision, that's based on the best input and advice, not only from General Lukic but from the heads of these other entities or organizational units because they proposed who the people should be, right? So the minister is making an informed, intelligent decision based on input from all those people, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No additional proof is sent to the minister because it goes without saying that before a proposal is sent out consultations had already taken place and that the candidate put up -- does meet all the requirements and is capable of carrying out all the tasks that he would be entrusted with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see in your preparations for testifying here the decision from 16 June 1998 to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism? It's a similar document to this P1811, but it was from June of 1998. Did you see that one?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then in that one it indicated that the deputy head of the staff was David Gajic, who we understand was from RDB; among others listed were Milorad Lukovic, who we know by the nickname Legija, as assistant head for operations; Lieutenant-Colonel Zivko Trajkovic, as assistant head for special anti-terrorist units. Did you know that they had been named to the staff in 1998?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for all the mentioned officers, I know them personally. I did not know that they were members of the staff. I knew that in certain stages they were engaged either like I or in some more official form, but I did not come across any of them in Kosovo because I arrived later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me move onto something else. You were shown an exhibit yesterday, 6D475, which was dated I think the 13th of June, 1999, and this one has a signature block for Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic. Now, you told us as far as you knew he was not a member of the MUP staff at that time, in June of 1999, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know he was not a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then Mr. Lukic went on to ask you: "Do you know of any other instances when documents or dispatches were being sent from the staff by people who were not members of the staff?" Even though in the heading we still had ministry staff. Your answer was: "Yes, I know of such instances." Now, you did tell us about a dispatch and an amendment that you had drafted, I believe, but we'll talk about that one in a minute. That's the one about getting information about unidentified dead bodies. But apart from that, can you tell me about any other specific instances where documents were being sent from the staff by people who were not members?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to that dispatch of mine, I mentioned yet another document, a document that was sent by Dragan Ilic, and I think when you were questioning me a few minutes ago about "saniranje," that is the document that I worked on too, that's the document that I know about. I think I sent yet another document or actually I'm sure that I sent yet another document, but it was towards the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us -- pardon me. You told us that with regard to Exhibit P1188, that's a one to which there was an amendment sent out the same day, the only change had to do with unidentified bodies as opposed to all the bodies. You recall the one I'm talking about? I see you're nodding your head yes, but I need you to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that is our exhibit P1188. My question to you is: What was the source of your authority to issue that document basically on behalf of the MUP staff of which you were not then yet a member? Did you have some written permission from General Lukic or some oral permission ahead of time or did you discuss this one specifically with him or did you just do it? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already explained that but it will be no problem for me to repeat all of that yet again. I was tasked with the following. I was supposed to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you repeat all that again, can you just answer my specific question. Did you have any specific oral or written permission from General Lukic to issue that kind of document, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had neither oral nor written permission, and I didn't need one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us why you didn't need one.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when the document is being registered in the log, which in itself is a credible document, it is also noted down who sent the document. It was the staff log-book and it was there so that I didn't have to go to Belgrade to register that in the UKP book. In -- that's why I sent it with the heading of the staff, with General Lukic's signature, and it was registered under that number as the UKP being the sender of that dispatch registered at the staff. In case of need or misunderstanding, we know who sent it and measures can be undertaken. Therefore, I didn't need any separate authorisation on the part of General Lukic to use the log-book and the communication devices or means that we only had at our disposal at the time. In some other conditions I would have used the communication channels of the criminal police department, but there were no conditions in place for that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, help me if you can with a question I have about the numbering of dispatches. That exhibit, P1188, is listed as dispatch number 145 dated the 28th of May, 1999, and I think the amendment is also the same day and it appears to have the number 145-A, can which I assume means amendment to 145. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, where does the number 145 come? Is that just a sequential number from the beginning of the year in 1999, so this is 145th one sent in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the 145th document in 1999 or the 145th document in June, or rather, May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But can we relate that number to the MUP staff or does that number, 145, refer to something back in Belgrade where you came from? Do you understand my question? Is this 145 in the log-book for MUP staff? Please, sorry.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the number in the MUP staff log-book. If it had been in the log-book of the UKP, the number would have been different. Possibly before this particular number and this document, the other documents also had to do with the work of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, where does it say on this document that it comes from the UKP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nowhere in the document does it say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the context and the text it can be concluded that it was sent by the UKP, and you can see that from the signature. In the heading it is not there. We only see the MUP staff there because that was the prescribed heading. I cannot change that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that prescribed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legal regulation in terms of headings in the bylaws of the UKP, the police -- criminal police administration, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what do these bylaws say that prevent you from identifying that it's the UKP that's sending this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot appear as the sender, since I used the log-book of the dispatches of the staff. When you use the log-book, you always use the staff heading. Other people can send documents such as General Stevanovic, Ilic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From a common sense point of view that would suggest that the whole object of this system is to conceal the truth rather than to make things clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think your remark stands. The whole system was aimed at those who are familiar with how it works. By mere chance it is you who have now encountered this problem. Another thing is that the book is a public document and you can see very well who sent what dispatch when, and anyone who can -- who wants to see that can. Of course I don't mean public outside the police domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do we have that book, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And have you tried to get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's part of our previous RFAs cover -- it would have covered that kind of log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are times, Mr. Gagic, when it has been difficult for this Tribunal to get documents to put the whole picture together. That may not apply in this case, I don't know, but it's just a possibility. Can we see the -- where this you say is signed by the UKP or by you? And you'll tell me it's a dispatch and it's not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think yesterday he explained he signed the original, but this document we have is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're right, but this is the one we have, Mr. Gagic. Where do I tell from this document that it's a UKP document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'll have to take my word for it in terms of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we can't tell from what we have in front of us that this is UKP; is that the position? What's your answer so that it's recorded, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is: Based on the document we have before us that one cannot see that the document was sent on behalf of the UKP via the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, to be sure I understand correctly, yesterday you explained that the copy we have is not the original copy, right? That's not the original?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But on the original you signed and you put "za" or "for" Sreten Lukic on the original, right? You'll have to answer out loud. I'm sorry. I see you nodding your head, but we need --

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the format is not the same. This went through a distribution machine for dispatches. It was in the form of a report, standard form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And since that time that you originally signed it and before it was sent out and during your time working on the KiM dossier, have you ever seen the original again?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen the original again. I do think I came across a copy, although I'm not certain whether it was a copy of this dispatch or of another dispatch which I sent perhaps a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where the original might be today?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the original was preserved, it should be with the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us a moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I think, if I understood your testimony yesterday, there was another one that had sort of a submission situation, that was Exhibit 6D874, if I could hand you a hard copy of that one. And this is dated the 6th of May, 1999, and you told us yesterday that regarding whose name is typed at the end of this document we see it as Sreten Lukic. You said: "As in the previous case and this was a general rule head of staff, Major Sreten Lukic and it was subsequently signed by whoever happened to be sending the circular out. Any recipients would know this is the person informing them and this is the person sharing information with them so the situation is perfectly identical. It's just the header that was used was the header of the MUP staff. The fact is that General Ilic was in Kosovo at the time and this was to keep him from going back to Belgrade." So this exhibit, 6D874, which we have with the typed signature of Sreten Lukic, is it your evidence that it was actually signed by General Ilic in the original? Sorry, you'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is this one that you helped draft?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this document has to do with the plan for "saniranje" of the terrain, I think that's how it was taken as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see this is dated the 6th of May, the day before that 7th of May meeting, that we saw on P1996 at the beginning of my cross-examination of you. Isn't this document the plan regarding terrain that General Ilic was talking about in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what I said. The only document I am familiar with is this document, in the drafting of which I took part. As for the other document pertaining to the plan of "saniranje" of the terrain, I'm not familiar with that. I think it wasn't clarified sufficiently in the minutes we saw. I don't know of any other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you telling me you didn't understand when we were going through that earlier that the plan that General Ilic was talking about was this one that you helped draft, that he signed, and that was sent out the day before? You didn't understand that when we were talking about it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understood that you thought there was another document. I don't know whether there is one. There may well be, but if it doesn't exist then General Ilic had this document in mind that was sent to all departments of crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Really, Mr. Gagic, you -- in the beginning I asked you about what this reference was, it said: "A plan of restoring territory has been compiled and distributed to all the SUP UKPs." Isn't that this plan in 6D874? This is a plan of restoring territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if another plan exists. I have never seen it. In case it does not exist, then this is the plan General Ilic was referred to at the meeting on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of course it is and why didn't you say that when I was asking you about it before? You said you didn't think such a plan existed. You helped draft it and sent it out the day before, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. Go back to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see in item number 4 of this document it also makes reference to the provisions of Article 218 which I asked you about when we were looking at the meeting of 7 May, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the main question I wanted to ask you about this was again you said this was an identical situation, so I take it this not a document for which you or General Ilic had written or oral permission from General Lukic to send out under the MUP staff header, right, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where the original of this one is with General Ilic's signature?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't ever see it again after the 6th of May, 1999, not during your time working on the KiM dossier or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the document. I saw him sign the document in front of me and it was to be distributed, then we split, I went on an assignment and he remained at the staff. After that time, I did not see the document. I wasn't working with that part of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You said that this was a general rule. It is formalised in a document or a manual somewhere, this practice?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a manual regulating and defining the names of organizational units of the MUP and the headers. As far as I know, as regards auxiliary bodies it is not mentioned there; however, the principal organizational units are included. In practice the same headers are used as the headers of other organizational units of similar composition, which is something that we can clearly see from this document. Be not confused by the number 21, it's another, different, book of confidential mail; the book I used was a general one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. So the one that you used in Exhibit P11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in Exhibit P1118 [sic], that had dispatch 145 and 145-A. We see this one as the number 12A-21?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say that's just because that was in a different dispatch log because this involved confidential documents of the MUP staff; is that right? You nodded your head, but I need an oral response.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in terms of this practice of being able to have a dispatch sent out with the MUP staff header by someone who was not a member of the MUP staff, I understand you say you were able to do it and General Ilic was able to do it. I mean, how far did that go? Could anybody from the MUP in Belgrade who happened to be in town come in and have a dispatch sent out with a MUP header or did you have to hold a certain rank or a certain position to be able to do that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no limit. It was defined by the need [as interpreted] at the moment. It wasn't foreseen for only generals, colonels, or majors to be able to do that; it depended on the urgency and necessity to forward documents ASAP. I was calling a meeting for the next day here. Most of those dispatches were sent by couriers. There was no time for me to go to Belgrade to work on it. It all depended on what needed to be done and what a certain dispatch refers to. Junior as well as senior officers were able to use the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You explained to us earlier how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on there are a couple of things to be clarified. Line 12 on page 33 should be P1188 rather than 1118, I think. And also I think the answer to the last question, that's line -- page 34, line 1, on my transcript which may not be identical to everyone else's, it was defined by the -- I think the witness said functional need at the moment rather than simply need at the moment. Do you recollect if that's what you actually said, Mr. Gagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And that's correct, it should be 1188.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think you explained earlier that the recipients of these documents would know who it came from even though it only said MUP staff and General Lukic at the bottom, right? Again you'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that because of the contents of the document they would answer who it was coming from?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly based on the content. When a dispatch arrives from the staff to the secretariat, it has eight or nine organizational units. Sometimes it is addressed in particular to what unit, but sometimes it also says the chief of SUP. He gets acquainted with the contents, and then depending on the type of issue he forwards that to the competent unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned a prosecutor, Mr. Hartman. It wasn't clear, but Mr. Hartman's a prosecutor in Kosovo I think with the UN. He's not a prosecutor here in The Hague with this Tribunal, right? Again, you'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said an international prosecutor, which is precisely what he used to do in Kosovo, but not anymore, I think. When I said international I didn't mean the ICTY, I meant the UNMIK judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And the last thing I wanted to ask you related to your testimony yesterday about interviewing Mr. Protic. You said you conducted an interview with Bozidar Protic in relation to his testimony when he was summoned to testify before the Hague Tribunal. Now, my notes indicate that you interviewed him I think around the 4th of June, 2001, or maybe you're referring to an interview with Protic that was done on the 27th of August, 2002. But those are the only two that I'm aware of, does that ring a bell for you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 2002 is more likely to be the case than 2001. I can't remember when exactly I talked to Protic, but I'm convinced that it was in 2002 because in 2001 I think it was Karleusa that talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I'm interested in though is your comment that you said it was in relation to his testimony when he was summoned to testify before the Hague Tribunal. My knowledge is he wasn't summoned to testify in front of this Tribunal until sometime in 2006, I think. So is that correct? Did you testify -- did you interview him in connection or in relation to his testimony when he was called to testify here?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't interview him when he was summoned to testify. I interviewed him when his obligation was veiled to preserve official secrets and when he had been summoned for an interview by the ICTY local office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that standard practice, to interview witnesses who have been called to speak to The Hague Tribunal representatives and a waiver has been sought?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a way it was standard practice simply because officials of the Ministry of the Interior were entitled to receive legal assistance, technical assistance, depending on their choice when they went to those interviews. We would call them and secondly we conducted talks to see if their potential evidence had anything to do with anything related to the waiver itself. So the taking of those statements was based on that. We did not lean on any of the witnesses; quite the contrary, in fact. Most of them, as far as what they stated to us at the time, repeated the same thing when testifying in court. I think there are documents showing that, and if need be I'm sure we can deliver those documents to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I didn't ask you if anybody leaned on them, but were you just anticipating that I might?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't anticipating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm sorry I went a little over, but I'm finished with my questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Very short one. I'd like to have P1824 on the e-court, please. We need page -- this is code on criminal procedure, and we need page 8 -- 15, actually, Article 218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I withdraw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you a question about the fact that Article 218 was something that people were adamant about. What is Article 218 of the Law on Criminal Procedure that then applied about?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the very first sentence you can tell what it's about. It talks about the circumstances that a suspect is to be interviewed about, the term here is suspect, but we use the term perpetrator. So it's about how an interview is to be conducted in order to prove the commission of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about paragraph 2, what is the first thing that is communicated?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grounds for suspicion against him, that is the first thing that is communicated. A perpetrator is informed of the reasons he has been brought in for. He's also told about any evidence that exists against him incriminating him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about paragraph 8 or item 8?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same as the previous law and any law so far, no coercion, no use of force in order to obtain a confession.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about item 10, paragraph 10? We don't have time to go through all of it now.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there has been any violation of Articles or paragraphs 8 and 9 of this article in the presence of counsel -- my copy is very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No court ruling can be based on any statement made by an accused, that's what it says. And my question to you is: Where did this law apply, in which territory?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. During the air-strikes and the state of war, in addition to this law what also applied was a decree extending the powers of the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What remains to be seen, is the exhibit that is to blame for all this confusion as to what the plan was and what it wasn't 6D874, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter is not certain whether it's 874 or 814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it 874 or 814, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 874, Your Honour. 6D874.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I talked to you about this, Mr. Hannis talked to you about this particular exhibit, this is a dispatch. You confirmed that you were involved in the compiling of this dispatch. It was signed by General Ilic. We shall be requiring page 2, or rather, the last page of this version. The English is gone. Can you please read the last sentence, the very last sentence of that document. They're about to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm waiting for too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately inform the MUP and the crime police administration of the results of the undertaken activities from the mentioned plan and supply statistical and analytical data on the 1st and the 15th of each month."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This plan shall come into effect immediately."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So is this a plan?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, please go to the sentence at item 7.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Undertake all measures and activities pursuant to the provisions of the law, or rather, secretariat chiefs are responsible for the realization of the envisaged activities and UKP crime police department chiefs are tasked with their direct realization."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you see this item?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as it is. I see it as a plan concerning measures and steps to be taken about this plan of taking more urgent steps to shed light on crimes, but it's also about unidentified corpses being found, how they're forensically examined and identified, if they are buried there is to be an exhumation and this is the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So who is in charge of this activity?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime police department, that's what it says, isn't it? The reporting is to be done vis-a-vis the UKP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gagic. Thanks for testifying. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, would you read again, please, slowly the paragraph that begins: "Immediately inform ..." It's the second-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. "Immediately inform the MUP and the crime police administration of the results of the undertaken activities from the mentioned plan and supply statistical and analytical data on the 1st and the 15th of each month."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reference there is to two organizations or organizational units perhaps, the MUP and the crime police administration. So what do you understand by the MUP in that context?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reference to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the word "staff" there in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because it was read -- we asked for it to be read twice and the word "staff" was not read to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'm sorry, Your Honours, if I may be of assistance actually, the witness read MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't suggest otherwise, Mr. Zecevic, and I particularly asked because I was keen to know if the word "staff" was there. All right. That clarifies the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, looking again at the document on the screen and picturing in your mind the original, which you say was signed by General Ilic, in what form was the name Major-General Sreten Lukic applied to that document? Was it as we see it here, typewritten, or was it applied in some other way?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the original document was compiled, and this is what it looks like, as shown here, what you found in the signature line was always the name of whoever was in charge of the unit mentioned in the document's header. Regardless of what organizational unit from my crime police administration was sending --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is a much more basic one, and that is: How was the name actually placed on the paper? Was it typewritten? Is it handwritten? Is it a stamp? Or is it some other way of applying the name Major-General Sreten Lukic to the document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as shown here, it's typewritten, they use an electrical typewriter or a mechanic one something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence to us. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is the next witness Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can do that after the break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] I need help from the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, you have an amended statement in front of you pursuant to a Court order yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones in the courtroom please be turned off. There is an awful amount of background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're going to have to start that again because the interpreters are having a problem. Someone's microphone is apparently on, either that or yours is somehow or other being disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
