utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, we're facing a certain amount of technical difficulty, therefore, I have to repeat my question. Suppose I were to ask you the same questions today as the ones you answered in your statement, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are now tendering Mr. Paponjak's statement, 6D1603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, the document in front of you, is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. How many paragraphs does it now have? I don't think I've actually been given the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The number of paragraphs are the same, only the paragraphs that have to be redacted are black now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. I can deal with that myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, for the sake of the record, can you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Radovan Paponjak, born on the 1st of May, 1948, in the Rudo. That is where I completed my elementary school education. I went to a secondary school in Foca, it was a teacher training school, it was in Uzice that I completed an academy for teachers, and then prevention and resocialization of persons with disturbances to their social behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you know, your statement was redacted or amended in part. My questions to you today will be very short and will focus on a limited range of matters. My first question: Were there any kidnappings in Pec municipality by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were abductions by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not just Pec municipality but also the Pec SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, the Pec SUP as well, meaning all the other municipalities covered by the Pec SUP, those abductions increased at one point in time 1998, May, June, and July specifically. At the time a total of 19 persons were abducted over such a short period of time, ten of them Serb, and nine Albanians, persons of Albanian ethnicity. There was a large number of abductions at roughly the same time next year, 1999, after the peace forces, peacekeeping forces had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any killings, were there any attacks by the KLA on the Serb settlements in the area covered by the Pec SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this was a particularly difficult problem jeopardizing the security situation in that area. There were killings which caused fear to arise among people living there. People would be killed in their own front yards, they would be killed by travelling. For example, Zorica Belic in Stepenica Klina municipality, he was killed in his own front yard. Mr. Vasic, for example, who was from the Kosovska Mitrovica area, he was waylaid and killed. There was another serious incident that affected the people living in the area, the shooting of Lazarevic, a young boy aged 16 whom the terrorists took away from his home and shot or executed outside his home. This is an incident that was publicised in the local papers and this caused the people living in the area to feel a huge amount of unrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was the situation at its most difficult concerning the security aspect, and I'm talking about the area covered by the Pec SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The most difficult situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, throughout 1998 in the so-called Baranjski Lug area comprising a number of villages, such as Celopek, Baran Rasic, and then further afield in the Klina area, a place called Kijevo settled by Serbs for the most part and it ended up isolated from the remaining sections of the area. You couldn't go there and you couldn't leave without exposing yourself to danger. One couldn't travel through the Rugovska Klisura area because the terrorists were attacking anyone making their way through and then Istok, Vrelo village, and Stari Dvorani and those areas too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Serbs in 1998, did they begin to leave certain areas covered by the Pec SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: It was precisely this kind of situation that left Serbs leaving their villages, quite a number of Serbs, from this very area, the Baranjski Lug area. They moved to Pec, those who had families there. Some left for Sumadija, which is in Serbia proper, in central Serbia as a matter of fact, or to Montenegro. People took refuge wherever they could. It wasn't just Serbs leaving the area. There were Albanians leaving as well who were facing problems with the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is Lodja and what is typical of that place at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Lodja is a settlement, it's on the outskirts of Pec because Pec and Lodja are now joined practically. At the time the terrorists had a particularly important stronghold in that village. They had built-up trenches, connecting trenches, gun-fire nests and fortifications. They even put up or established a gun-fire nest at the top of a mosque. The situation was dangerous. There was a danger to all the Serbs living there or anyone attempting to make their way into Lodja, even our own access to that settlement was limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about this Pec suburb, were there any attacks that occurred there and who was subjected to those attacks? Are you aware of any incidents that were typical?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were always skirmishes there and shoot-outs. Sometime early in July 1998, in the morning hours, homes were attacked belonging to the Josevic family. The Pec SUP got wind of this and a unit was immediately dispatched to the extent that men were available at all to provide assistance. It was not a very strong unit. There were only so many men available and on duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what happened next once this unit had been dispatched to Lodja?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: They managed to reach the Vujosevic homes. The terrorists had given up on the attack that they had launched because an end was put to their attack. These officers who arrived there talked to members of the Vujosevic family and the unit was now on its way back. On their way back the terrorists set up an ambush and opened fire on the vehicles that the police were using on their way back. They used rifles and hand-held launchers in the course of this attack. A shell hit one of the police vehicles killing two policemen and wounding many. There was a skirmish and the unit was soon assisted by another unit that came to their rescue from the Pec SUP. Those killed and wounded were evacuated, and two members of the Pec SUP, two police officers Captain Srdjan Perovic and police officer Mirko Rajkovic were abducted by the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was something you told me about yesterday, paragraph 21, there is another amendment to be made. It says the petrol station owner, Nasiri petrol, this is page 7 in the B/C/S. How should this read?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The owner of the petrol station and then quotation marks "Nasiri," deriving from the name Nasir, "Nasiri" petrol. This is what the petrol station was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what exactly is the amendment to be made? After Berisha this word should be inserted, should it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The name of that petrol station is petrol, but Nasiri petrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to go back to this. You said that two police officers were abducted during this attack. Do you know what became of them? Did you ever learn?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Following an anti-terrorist operation once the terrorists had been pushed back from that village, the bodies of these two colleagues of mine were found. There was a post mortem establishing that they had been killed. Prior to their deaths, however, they had been tortured, parts of their bodies were severed, and they had been mutilated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence that the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, could you repeat the last sentence of your answer, please, the interpreter did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there's a case file in the Pec SUP covering this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, what about the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, is there information there, reliable information, on various incidents that occurred in the area covered by the Pec SUP and what is this kind of information about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there is, both in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and in the Pec SUP. This is about the killings of Serb civilians, of Albanian civilians, and persons belonging to other ethnicities. There is information about mistreatment of Serbs, Albanians, all civilians, other ethnicities too, about abductions that occurred, abductions of civilians again, belonging to all the different ethnic groups there. It's about terrorist attacks, it's about attacks on the police and the army. There is information about the air-strikes against the area, its installations, facilities, settlements. There is information about anything that was security-related and that was going on in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at a later stage process this information?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was more processing at a later stage. Certain documents were compiled after those incidents. Crime scene investigation reports were drawn up by investigating judges, appropriate official notes were drawn up, criminal complaints were filed, and so on. By the time we had no choice but to leave the area, those documents were transported in a number of ways. We did whatever we could, and we used whatever we could to take these documents to a number of different towns in Serbia, specifically to Kragujevac and to other towns in that general area. Once we had been forced to move out of our forward command post in Kragujevac - if I'm referring to the Pec SUP - we started to gather those documents. These documents would be unloaded as soon as they arrived. The case files were kept separate. We first had to make sure all of the case files were complete, we had to assign numbers to them, and then we had to organize these case files all over again. We organized all this documentation and made sure the system was the same as the one we had applied back in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who gave the order, "nalog," to process all this information?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The documents were organized and classified with no particular order. This was something that we had to do and we had to organize our own records. At a later date we received an order from the Ministry of the Interior to organize our documentation in line with a methodology that had never before been used in the SUP. This was an order from the ministry and they prescribed a methodology for us to apply according to which we organized all this material by chapters. It was for that purpose that I set up a team to deal with this. The job took months. Heads of departments were involved in this work, especially those of the internal organizational SUP units, people who were actually heads of those departments at the time, and if there were any changes to be made new people that were involved, police station commanders, each in relation to their own areas, and then chiefs of certain sectors that were part of the secretariats, analysts, IT people, and people who provided different kinds of technical support. I was in charge of the overall effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to all the parameters that were provided, are there individual case files?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: That's the way we worked. First individual case files were organized and then lists of events were compiled according to the relevant methodology, then statistics were worked on, that is to say tables were made. Finally, a general piece of information was compiled which could be used by anyone who would be looking at this for the first time to get some basic information. If this person would be interested in individual cases, then he could find them through tables, through lists, and through individual case files.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of some of these surveys, lists, do you know that off the top of your head?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, these chapters, if I can call them that, are classified, categorised, and marked by numbers, or rather, letters. In the Ministry of the Interior this was called the KiM dossier, the dossier of Kosovo and Metohija. Chapter A pertains to security-related events resulting in death pertaining to armed conflicts in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999. A is the letter that is the designator of that chapter, but the relevant SUPs have Roman numerals. So A/III means that it is that chapter resulting in death --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This evidence that the witness is giving at this point is going into the documents that were excluded yesterday from the Defence 65 ter list and which were excluded from this witness statement. So I don't feel it's appropriate for him to be going into this specific evidence. It is precisely the paragraphs that were removed. We're omitting reference to the exhibit numbers, but the evidence is the same. This was particularly -- I think it was paragraph 25 which was redacted from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's not 6D614 that this relates to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's obvious that I'm not using any documents. I'm asking this witness whether he remembers what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, and what's the purpose of that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be able to include the documents that were left out of his statement. If he remembers his work I don't understand why he wouldn't be able to tell us what he remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This specific evidence was in paragraph 25 and it's one of the paragraphs that was redacted precisely because the Chamber considered that we weren't given sufficient notice that these -- I understand the actual exhibits that are underlying this evidence are not being used, but the evidence itself has been redacted from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do not think what has occurred so far in this chapter of the evidence circumvents the order that was made. The evidence relating to the system that was used may well be relevant in a wider context and in particular at a later stage of the case. So, Mr. Lukic, as long as you confine yourself to the system and keep away from the particular incidents for which the details have not been provided because of the redaction of the statement, then we will allow you to continue to pursue this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm exactly trying just to establish the system, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, could you please tell us what this system was and could you give us the names of these individual parts that you produced?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: In this chapter A there are security-related incidents resulting in death, A/III is the designation for the Pec SUP. This contains information about the relevant events. I can dictate the full name for you, information on security-related events resulting in death in relation to armed conflicts in the territory of the SUP of Pec during the course of 1998 and 1999. The next document is a survey consisting of tables. Now, we have two such surveys one is a survey of incidents resulting in death in terms of territory, and the other survey has to do with these same incidents but in relation to different time-periods. The next document is a list of security-related events resulting in death pertaining to armed conflicts in the territory of the SUP of Pec during the period of 1998 and 1999. The next part are individual case files that are also marked individually, each and every one of them. Chapter P -- chapter B has to do with crimes committed against Albanians in 1998 and 1999. That chapter has the same documents, that is to say this general document or information. Then there is a table based on the time-periods involved, then a table based on the territory involved, then there is a list of crimes committed against Albanians and there are individual case files for each and every crime committed against Albanians. Subsequently a chapter B asterisk was introduced, this was done by the MUP and it has to do with crimes committed against Serbs during 1998 and 1999. This chapter also contains information about these events, a table based on time-periods, a table based on the territory involved, a list, and individual case files. Chapter D pertains to security-related events pertaining to kidnappings and missed persons. It also has documents of its own as well as a piece of information about these events, then also tables based on time-periods involved and based on the territory involved. Then there is a list of these events and individual case files. I have to point out that this chapter cannot be fully defined yet because the final number of kidnapped persons remains unknown as well as the fate of kidnapped and missing persons. I think that it is noteworthy in relation to chapter A that perhaps it was formulated in a rather clumsy way. Perhaps we did this in a slightly different way without understanding. In chapter A we recorded all the deaths that we found out about, regardless of whether they have to do with deaths that are the result of armed conflicts or deaths that are the result of homicide or some kind of suspicious death where we did not know what it was all about in the first place. Then chapter A includes descriptions of all crimes resulting in death, regardless of whether they have to do with the armed conflict or not. So the information from this chapter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Paponjak, that's enough for the moment and Mr. Lukic can ask you if there's any more detail he requires on this. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I think that suffices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, for our purposes here today what you've said so far is sufficient. Thank you very much. In addition to A, B, D, were there --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were other chapters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give us the numbers, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, there were chapters that pertained to police conduct, then pertaining to the Roma, then there was a chapter on the effects of bombing and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. And who compiled these surveys, these lists, and these pieces of information?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: As for the SUP of Pec, this was completely done by the employees of the Pec SUP, so these were the crime police employees, the police employees and the other employees that dealt with this, that is to say the analysts, the IT people, and the appropriate services.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who headed them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I headed this particular team as chief of the secretariat of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we're going to move onto something completely different, the presence of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the time involved. Do you know whether terrorists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment before you ... Sorry. Please continue, Mr. Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did terrorists launch attack while the Kosovo verification was in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it did. At one point in time, or rather, in one period before the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived there weren't any such attacks, and the attacks started and intensified precisely during the presence of the verification mission, which really hit us hard. During the stay of the verification mission in Kosmet in the territory of the SUP of Pec 61 terrorist attacks took place, namely, seven against buildings and 54 against persons. In all these attacks, or rather, members of the Kosovo Verification Mission were informed about all these attacks, they attended on-site investigations whenever they wanted to, it was their choice, they had this option of choosing whether they would attend or would not attend. I can say that the terrorists were not very picky as far as targets were concerned, so they attacked ethnic Albanians as well and ethnic Albanians got killed too. For the most part attacks took place on roads or by way of breaking into houses. They openly fired at vehicles that were moving along roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Pec itself were there any attacks and what would be an attack that particularly disturbed the public?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were several attacks in Pec, primarily at -- against cafes and restaurants. A glaring case was the attack against the Slavica cafe and then in December, I think it was the 14th of December, 1998, in the evening hours near the high school in Pec, there were some young men who were sitting in a cafe called Panda and terrorists fired at them using automatic rifles. On that occasion six young men were killed on the spot and a few were wounded. Of course this affected people deeply and was an additional complication in terms of the situation in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you already have this statement I keep leaping from one topic to another. So now I'm going to ask you whether in the territory of the SUP of Pec there were established check-points and what are check-points?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Check-points are one of the ways in which the police operate. I would define a check-point as a stationary patrol or a patrol that is fixed at one particular point, at one particular location. Check-points are organized in order to check on persons and vehicles. Persons are checked with a view to identifying and finding the perpetrators of crimes and vehicles are checked with a view to finding objects that were used to commit crimes because in the contemporary world crime, as a rule, is on wheels, smuggling, transportation of goods that are the result of crimes and so on. Check-points are a customary way of operation in Serbia ever since I've been in the service that is to say, since 1970, perhaps this was the case earlier on as well and these check-points do yield certain results. In the territory of the SUP of Pec there were some check-points. Throughout my stay there, there were check-points. We even had some customary traffic check-points, they can be permanent, they can be there from time to time, they can be traffic check-points, and there can be combined check-points in terms of the structure of their work. The combined ones are the best where traffic policemen check on vehicles and drivers and a member of the crime police who's at the check-point deals with aspects of his own work to see whether there are perpetrators of crimes that are trying to pass that way or whether there are objects related to crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are there check-points in Belgrade and Pristina nowadays?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There are, in the outskirts of Belgrade there are check-points, they are different from the ones we had, they have booths with everything else that is needed for extended stays of employees. When leaving Belgrade in any direction, you should encounter such a check-point. I know there were some in Pristina and there were some in Pec at the moment of my departure under the protection of the UN. I saw in the centre of Pec that their check-points were different from ours since they were inside barbed wire. At the time I was leaving Pec, the peacekeeping forces had already come in. While we worked there we had no barbed wire check-points. We had a different type of security, traffic security. First we would impose signs in order to reduce the speed with a warning that there is a police check-point nearby, and when terrorist attacks commenced we had in-depth check-point security in order to secure our personnel. We would have other people in depth trying to prevent terrorists from attacking check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1999 in Pec were there any VJ check-points?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the territory of SUP Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, during a period of time. In the territory of the Pec SUP in the settlement of Pec itself I know there were two such locations. In Ramiz Sadiku Street and Miladin Popovic Street. Then there were some in the area of Istok in a location called Rudnik. Then in Djurakovac and in Bijelo Polje we held joint or combined check-points. At Savine Vode, we had a permanent check-point, and for a while we were assisted by VJ members in providing security there from terrorists. We had some other check-points which were regular traffic check-points in town, in certain key intersections. They didn't have any particular signs, but we would just refer to, for example, the Durija [phoen] check-point and the policemen who were supposed to go there knew exactly what it was and where to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Pec and in Istok were there any members of military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were. In Pec there was the 177th Military Territorial Detachment, in Istok there was the 69th Military Territorial Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to your statement, there is something there that I would like to hear from you. What happened in Pec on the 27th and the 28th of March, 1999? Tell us what you know personally.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: At the time I was the chief of the traffic police. We were in charge of controlling and regulating traffic. I don't particularly recall those two days as such, but I do know that at that time after the air-strikes began there was more movement of vehicles and pedestrians along the roads. That was causing certain problems in terms of traffic regulation. Around those days I also moved about much more. I went into the field more frequently in order to direct the work of patrols. Traffic cannot be regulated partially. You need to encompass an entire area. Those who know that know that traffic is regulated along axes and roads and it cannot be regulated partially but even across state borders. There were villages surrounding Pec where we had our patrols, and they were reporting that there was an increased movement of all sorts of vehicles, freight vehicles, tractors, as well as an increased number in pedestrians. All of those were pouring into the city towards its centre. Realizing that there will be masses of people, I went into the field, especially to the places where there were most people assembled to try and redirect the movement if necessary. This is how I recall those particular events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend a gathering of citizens in the centre of Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I did. I was in the centre of town myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any policemen in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were. We had our regular patrols at their usual points or posts. These were permanent areas for our traffic patrols. In most towns traffic is usually the worst in the centre, and as you move outside the settlement there is less and less traffic. In the centre itself we had patrols at three locations or points. At those three points we were trying to assist the movement of vehicles and passengers. I was in my vehicle and by that time there was no possibility to move inside the centre. I managed, however, to enter the centre with my vehicle since there was a certain space, a lane was left for the movement of vehicles. I was alone for the most part, I did not have a driver, since my job post was such, and I reached the building of the Municipal Assembly. Excuse me. There were many people, the centre was crowded. I did manage to reach the municipal building without any problems. I saw that those people were mainly Albanians, of course I don't know all of Pec's inhabitants, but during the eight years there I met a number of people. I saw some of my acquaintances there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the gathering addressed by anyone from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you address those gathered?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone address the gathering and who it was and in what way, did you understand what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were some speakers. I don't understand the Albanian language, maybe I know 10 or 20 words. I did hear some people speak. They were using a mouthpiece, a loudspeaker, but I couldn't make out what they were talking about. I did speak to some of my acquaintances there. There was this Albanian postman, and he told me that he was approached by a Serb asking for a certificate that some payment was made. He said, Well, this is what he finds important. He doesn't mind the bombs. He just wants me to issue him with a receipt. This is the conversation we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone force those people to go to the centre of town or did anyone force them to leave the centre of town on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, it was impossible. Let's discuss whether anyone forced them to leave. How many policemen would one need in terms of policemen or soldiers to force such a mass of people to leave? Or vice versa, to force them into the centre of town. First you would have to gather them from all around the town and the villages we -- that we did not even enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why were you not entering certain villages?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: We were unable to because they were occupied or controlled by the terrorists. If we tried going to those villages, they opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From what time did you stop going to those villages and can you tell us the names of some of those villages that the police could not go to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Several month or half a year, for example, from the fall before, and those were most of the villages surrounding Pec, Istok, and Klina inhabited by Albanians who were Muslim. Most of those villages were terrorist strongholds. We could go to some other villages inhabited by Catholic Albanians because their relationship with the terrorists was somewhat different and there weren't that many of them involved in terrorism. They even had problems because they refused to participate in that and the terrorists were targeting them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Except for your conversation with the postman, did you speak to anyone else? Did you manage to grasp why those people were leaving?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: People were asking me whether they can go to Montenegro, to Djakovica, or Pristina, and I found that strange. There was no restriction of movement for anyone. It wasn't clear to me why they were asking that. They also asked me whether they can use their vehicles to move. I told them that certainly they can use their vehicles as they wish. It all boiled to that particular topic, boiled down to that particular topic. They were also asking me whether they would be restricted in terms of movement if they tried to use the Kula mountain pass. I told them as far as I know that road was open. I saw several of my acquaintances. One of them I asked where he was going to. He said that he was going to his children and his wife who were in Germany. He was together with another acquaintance of mine who had a van. They wanted to go together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see the people boarding any buses in the centre of town? Was anyone forcing them to go on the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Buses could not reach the centre of town, that was the traffic regulation in place, no buses in the centre of town. All bus traffic at the time was still running pretty regularly, there were buses leaving for Belgrade and other parts of the country. You could go to Montenegro, Prizren, Djakovica, there were local buses as well as inter-city buses. People were using buses normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you or anyone else on the Serb side order that those people should be forced onto any buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Absolutely no. No one had ordered anything of the sort to me and I did not order that to my people. There was no reason for me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did it take for the centre of town to be empty? When did the crowd disperse?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I cannot say that the centre of town became empty. There were waves. People were coming and going and the whole thing lasted for several days. We also had crowds along all roads and both going and going out. Some were coming into town from Pristina and Djakovica as well as Kosovska Mitrovica. The critical point was the Kula mountain pass, since there are great elevations there, it was steep and the vehicles wouldn't be able to negotiate those frequently. They would stop around bends, there were tractors with trailers, the whole thing was a very difficult one. I moved along that road twice in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this Kula is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Kula is a mountain pass. I'm not very a maps, but it is between Pec and Rozaje in Montenegro, it is on that road. The elevation is at least 1400 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Paponjak. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Paponjak.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have just a few questions for you. Paragraph 79 of your statement you say that on the 12th of April you were sent from the headquarters of the Pec SUP to the OUP Istok. Can you just tell me what position you were in at the OUP Istok in this period from the 12th of April until the 11th of June, what kind of work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The OUP Istok is one of the organizational units of the Pec SUP. I was sent there to work for a certain period of time to help out at the OUP Istok without any kind of decision on that kind of an appointment, that is to say without specifying a particular type of job, as one of the more senior colleagues there with more experience, that is why there was no need to have a decision on appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 86 of your statement you say that on the 14th of April a commission came to Istok that had been set up through an order of the commander of the 3rd Army, the number is given there, it's a strictly confidential document, and the date is the 13th of April. Can you please tell me when it was that you first saw this document on the establishment of this commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I think that I saw this document only after the leaving the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the next paragraph, 87, of your statement, you say that this commission established beyond any doubt on the spot that there was no camp there as some misinformation had stated. I'm asking you whether you know that this commission after returning from Istok compiled some kind of a report about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what kind of a report this commission compiled but I know that they interviewed me while they were in Istok, what kind of a report was ultimately compiled is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 4D212 is this report and it has been admitted into evidence. Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Paponjak.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I am Djuro Cepic, and I appear for the defence of General Vladimir Lazarevic. You do have your statement in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will start my questions with referring to paragraph 71. My colleagues tell me that there is a transcript problem. Now it looks better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, the number again of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D212, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, in paragraph 71 you provided a description to the effect that there were many reserve members of the military who were there. Can you perhaps tell us whether you know whether these were people who were moving from their residences, their homes, to the mobilisation sites?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Paponjak, paragraph 72, you say that a number of criminals were mobilised in the reserve force who had committed serious crimes before that as well as disturbing public law and order. I assume that you draw that conclusion on the basis of your personal knowledge of particular individuals, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It's not only on that basis. We also have crime records and we know that; however, the fact remains that we did recognise certain people as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that as far as conscription is concerned, having a criminal record is of no consequence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And I assume that you know that most citizens who were males, regardless of whether they had a criminal record or not, were part of the reserve force of the military?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and no one can be free of this obligation regardless of whether they had committed a crime in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic -- perhaps I should direct this to the witness. Does that apply to someone who's been convicted of rape or murder or serious injury to life and limb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really don't know now. I don't know what it was that they had been convicted for, but I do know that there were some there who had committed property-related offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, if we are to call these people criminals, did any one of them commit any one of these crimes while they were on the reserve force of the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I do not know of any such thing. I don't have any such information that one of these persons did something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 73, what you say here is that a number of criminals were self-mobilised, they put on uniforms and so on. You will agree with me that there were abuses of uniforms and insignia, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I remember this period. This was one of the problems that encumbered our work because a certain number of persons moved about in uniform, they were driving vehicles on which --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have that in the statement. We have all of it. I'm just asking you the following: Is this abuse of uniform by unauthorised persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move onto paragraph 74. Could we please call up in e-court 6D125. I would just like to tell you, Your Honours, that after March 1999 there are three numbers 6D125, 5D36, and P1208 respectively, it's the same document. Mr. Paponjak, we have an order of the -- from the commander of the Pec defence office, the date is the 30th of March, 1999. If we look at the first paragraph of this document the author of this document is not invoking any particular order. You will agree with me that this kind of order did not affect your work and the work of the police, rather, you worked independently of this and carried out your regular work and duties?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps know that this document was subsequently declared null and void by this very same structure upon orders from higher instances?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I saw this document considerably later, not in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 5D37, please. Could we please have that in e-court. Mr. Paponjak, here's the document, have you seen this before, not -- never mind.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move onto paragraph 76 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm trying to follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the point of that question? Does 5D37 relate to 6D125 in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the declaration of it being null and void?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, let us now deal with the municipality of Istok, or rather, the commander of the military territorial detachment, the 69th Detachment that is and the situation that prevailed there. Tell me, Mr. Paponjak, when the 7th Infantry Brigade arrived, did the situation calm down in the town of Istok?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it did, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know -- well, I don't know of other structures now in relation to the one that you're in, but do you know that the military detachment, or rather, this military territorial detachment was it subordinated to the military office of Pec, if you know you do tell us, and if not --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I really have to tell you that I don't know much about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. You will agree with me that your structure, that is to say the structure of the Ministry of the Interior, acted independently without the influence of any kind of staff or body in carrying out its duties on the basis of the law?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We have a specific law and a rule book on organization and other rules that regulate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And no influence was exercised over your work by the military territorial detachment in the sense of them issuing some kind of orders or tasks to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the transcript we have already tendered 5D374 dated the 23rd of April prohibiting any kind of establishment of staffs by the members of the Army of Yugoslavia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, paragraph 85, Colonel Cirkovic, commander of the 7th Infantry Brigade spoke about the return of displaced persons and about combat activities taking place near Lukavac. Was there high intensity in these combat activities in the area of Lukavac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Not at that time; however, all of us were highly concerned about these civilians because we didn't know what would go on or what would happen later. This was the defence area, as the colonel said, and persons should not be there, rather, they should be at safe locations that should be found for them. Later on there was heavy bombing throughout that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that there were fierce terrorist attacks there as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that happened too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, what about the members of the army, the members of the MUP, the members of civilian authorities, did they to their best to provide safe accommodation for civilians as well as food, aid, medicine, et cetera, outside combat areas?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, the Red Cross health institutions, social welfare institutions were involved in all of this. They got food, I know that personally because I moved about quite a bit in the area. I know people who were involved in that, even I personally gave some people tinned food and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Your Honours, this would be a convenient moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Paponjak, we break for lunch at this stage. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again in one hour at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, my last set of questions, perhaps even a single question. You testified about Lodja. I have a piece of footage dated the 16th of August, 1998, that I would like us to look at. Can that please be played in e-court, this is Defence Exhibit 5D1239. This is Lodja on the 16th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, are these the connecting trenches that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is just one portion of it. Of course the TV crew had no need to take it all in. I arrived in the village following this action because one had to re-establish a normal flow of traffic and for people to get on with their lives. I had to clear the roads and not just here. I arrived at the scene after several of those actions had taken place. The roads were blocked or cluttered. This is just part of the connecting trenches that were there and the weapons that were floating about that had been assembled by the time the TV crew got there. The gathering of those weapons had not been completed yet or the clearing of the roads for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We heard this was a police action. What I want to know is how long were these connecting trenches?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Kilometre-long trenches [as interpreted]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Paponjak. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify something more because in transcript it's not correctly as the witness said. With your leave, one more question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paponjak, it is not reflected in the transcript one kilometre or kilometres?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were each of the homes strongholds as it were?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I encountered some difficulty trying to pass by a house that was full of ammunition which at one point exploded and the sound of the blast could be heard although the action had been completed. The journalists were there and they heard it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions for you, Mr. Paponjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, had that exhibit been admitted before?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a part of it, two clips in relation to Malisevo and the village of Junik. The third part of this CD has just been shown, the last section has not been shown so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what happened in relation to the commentary in the other cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to Junik village during our own case we heard testimony of Veljko Odalovic and we tendered the transcript, the language of the video. My colleague Mr. Lukic and I still owe you the footage on, or rather, the footage on Malisevo was played when Andreja Milosavljevic was here, but I think Mr. Lukic took it upon himself to do the Malisevo transcript if I'm not mistaken. And if I may, with your permission, I can perhaps secure a transcript of what the journalist was saying in relation to Lodja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall admit the video without the sound, so we have -- unless the situation changes between now and the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Ms. Kravetz. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Paponjak.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to begin by asking you some questions about the events you described in Pec municipality in March of 1999. You told us during your evidence today in your statement that after the state of war was declared on 24th March VJ reserve forces were mobilised in the Pec area. Were regular VJ units also mobilised in -- to the Pec area in this period?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know. I know about the reserve forces because those were locals from Pec and the surroundings, those who came. I did not recognise any of the regular forces in town. I simply was in no position to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the reserve forces you are talking about or you spoke about earlier are local Serbs who were mobilised and they were assigned a uniform and weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why do you distinguish these persons as reservists from just the regular VJ units, how were you able to distinguish these were reservists and they were not just regular VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Because those were my neighbours, people who lived nearby, in my area, and now I saw them wearing uniforms. I knew that they were no regular soldiers, I knew they were not doing their regular military term because they were older - what I'm saying is over 18 or 19 years of age - and they were telling me that they were supposed to report to a mobilisation point and that's why I knew that they were reservists and no regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know who issued these persons with weapons and with uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, I know about police members. As I said a while ago, I don't really know much about all these military matters. It's not what I was trained for and it certainly wasn't my job. I did do my own regular military term, but after that I never had anything more to do with the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see. I understand. Were local Serbs also incorporated into the police once the state of war was declared, and I'm speaking particularly of Pec municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, some. We had our own reserve police which at the time was involved in something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would there be -- was there any distinction of staff between the regular policemen like yourself and these local reservists, reserve policemen which began working for the MUP once a state of war was declared? Was there any differentiation of tasks between the regular police officer and the reservist?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No. There was no apparent distinction. You couldn't draw a distinction if you looked at a patrol made up of regular police officers or one of reserve police officers. They wore the same uniform, they carried the same weapons, and they had the same tasks. It's just that reserve police officers could not perform their duties on their own, independently. They would also be monitored by regular police officers, and this is how patrols were made up. A regular police member was always in charge of a patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many local Serbs were mobilised and joined the police force once a state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was busy elsewhere at the time on a different job and it had nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. You told us in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear, what was the other job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was chief of the traffic police department, and that job had nothing to do with the police reserve forces. Other than that, as to how many members of the reserve police force were involved in this, this is something that should be easy enough to track down in various documents that I think exist. We certainly have this in our own reports. I can't tell you off the top of my head, not even a ballpark figure, but I'm sure the exact figure is somewhere or other in one of our documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can't assist us at all with a rough indication of the numbers involved in spite of all the activity you were involved in, in Pec itself at the early stages of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to engage in that sort of guess-work. What I'm saying is we had this information in our documents and this is in the public domain in the sense of not being confidential. It's just that I can't give you a ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect we don't have the document, so please try to help us as best you can. As I've indicated already today, we do sometimes have great difficulty getting documents from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one thing I can do is promise the Chamber that I will make sure to have this information forwarded to you, but unfortunately there isn't much more that I can say about that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, you have been able to tell us a considerable amount of the activities of VJ reservists in the town, criminals being associated with the VJ, but you can't tell us anything at all about numbers of police reservists mobilised in Pec at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said anything about any numbers, including those pertaining to the military reserve forces because I'm not really aware of those either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have been able to tell us, for example, there was a large presence of VJ reservists in towns and villages. You've told us that the reserve forces of the Yugoslav Army were mobilised in the Pec area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A number of criminals who had committed serious crimes in violations of law and order in the past were also mobilised into the VJ reserve force. A number of criminals were self-mobilised. So what concerns me is your unwillingness to tell us anything, give us any indication, even your impression of numbers of reservists being mobilised at that time. You're prepared to do it in respect of the army, why not the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can say to you that an insufficient number of people were mobilised because I had a constant manpower problem because I did not have enough traffic policemen. Not a sufficient number had been mobilised in my view. So if I were supposed to say something about that I would say that I did not have enough people mobilised in terms of my own liking because I really needed a lot more policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on this last issue, how many reservists were mobilised in your department, the traffic department? You said an insufficient number. Do you recall how many?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I think less than 30, I think, that is to say that I'm not sure. As for the number of people in my group, it was the commander of the police station who took care of that. I would have to provide an explanation so that the Court would understand why it is that I'm saying this. In my group it was traffic police work that was the main activity and the commander of the police station was in charge of that. Administrative work and work related to inspection in terms of the civilian part, that is to say the technical regulation of transport, driving lessons, the technical examination of vehicles, and so on, that was a different part of my service. I was the chief of both of these. I had heads of lines involved in different lines of work, so I don't know of anything very specific in any one of these cases. I can just talk about my general impression in terms of what it was that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you there. I was just asking about numbers. You said less than 30. Would it be fair to say in other departments was that number similar, around 30 or more than 30, do you know that, other departments of the Pec SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Possibly there may have been more, there may have been less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. You indicated today and also you referred to this in your statement starting at paragraph 55 that towards the end of March, 27th, 28th March, large crowds of Kosovo Albanians began pouring into the centre of the city and you said that you -- patrols of your department reported this to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you yourself went to the centre of Pec to see what was happening that day, when these large crowds of people were pouring into the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say large crowds were pouring or I think you said many people and it was crowded, approximately how many people were there in the centre of Pec towards the end of -- we're talking 27 March, do you recall? I mean are we talking thousands? Hundreds?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Thousands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know where these people were coming from, these thousands of Kosovo Albanians that had gathered in the centre of Pec, where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were people from Pec who I knew personally. According to the reports of patrols, on the basis of which I have this knowledge, there were people from the surrounding villages too. It's not that it was people from one village only. It is from the surrounding villages that they were pouring into town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So people were coming in from surrounding villages of Pec municipality and all heading in the direction of the town of Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these columns of Kosovo Albanians, they gathered I think you said in the centre of the town, that's where they were gathered?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So when you arrived there and you saw that thousands of people had gathered in the centre of Pec, what did you do exactly? What actions did you take?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Nothing. I stood there for a while, I talked to them, and then I went further on on the ground. I didn't spend two days there, but I didn't take any measures except for the fact that the patrols had the task of not allowing any bottlenecks. It was important for passengers in vehicles to move on, pedestrians and vehicles, that was difficult work. In the centre of town there was a patrol, in the centre towards the patriarchate and then towards the center towards Djakovica and the third one was towards the SUP of Pec, which is towards Mitrovica. These are the regular places where traffic police patrols were. And then further on, on the outskirts of town there was yet another patrol towards Vitomirica and then there was a patrol by the Drvni Kombinat the timber processing plant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you arrived there and you saw that these large crowds of people had gathered there. Did you contact, for example, the SUP chief to tell him what was happening in the centre of town or the deputy chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I informed the chief of SUP before I went there, the chief of SUP had been informed about the fact that columns were coming in and that there was a lot of commotion, and I said that I would be going to the centre to take measures so that traffic could go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you got there and you're saying that your only concern was to regulate traffic, you were faced with these crowds of Kosovo Albanians in the centre of town and you thought that the most important thing to do in that situation was to regulate traffic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you say in your statement that you were the highest-ranking member of your SUP there that day when these crowds of people gathered in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You also said earlier that your patrols were there from your department. Approximately how many police officers were present in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to work it out on the basis of the number of patrols involved. There were over 20, say between 20 and 30. I'm giving a rough approximation on the basis of the number of patrols and the number of men on each patrol, which is to say three per patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any VJ soldiers present in the centre of town when this was going on?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Any other armed personnel other than you and your 20 or so or 30 police officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any in the small streets, but there weren't any in the streets where I was moving. I know that police patrols of a general nature also carry out patrol activity, but these patrols were not the subject of my interest at that time. They were not there simply. It was only the traffic police patrols that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know why these persons had gathered there in such large crowds?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I found out about that from my conversations with certain individuals that I knew. I mentioned the postman that I talked to. I mentioned an acquaintance of mine as well who had said to me that he was supposed to leave Pec. The postman also told me that he was leaving Pec, and that is why he was saying this to me, that this man had asked him for a receipt in terms of his telephone bill or whatever it was. Then further on some people asked me whether they could go towards Montenegro, others asked me if they could go towards Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking is: Do you know the reason why such large crowds of people had gathered in the centre of town, 27th March? Why were those people there heading from all villages in Pec municipality to the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I did not understand you, actually. What do you mean by the reason why?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know why -- what was forcing these people or what were the reasons these people left their homes and headed towards the centre of the town of Pec on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know the exact reason. I can assume that the reason was the same like for the others who were leaving their homes. The Albanians came on that day or during the course of those days to the centre of town. Some Serbs were leaving without going into the centre of town, the reason was the same. I had requested from policemen who were requesting leave in order to take their families out of the area. So I can assume that the reasons were common to all. I don't know why each and every individual came there. We had a number of policemen who, although they were not granted leave left the area nevertheless. They did not report for work. They would drive their wives and children to Montenegro, for instance, to stay with their relatives or say to the other part of Serbia and they'd come back --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, but during your evidence today you said that these persons who had gathered in the centre of town were mostly Kosovo Albanians. You're saying the reasons were the same. What were those reasons? Why had these people gathered in such large numbers there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: When the bombing started -- I can tell you what my personal impression was. First of all, I could not believe that the bombing had actually started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you're being asked if you know the reason why these people had gathered in the centre of Pec. Now, you're a police officer in charge of trying to control the crowds to enable the traffic to move. It's difficult to imagine anyone better-placed than you to tell us why these people had come into Pec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I've been trying to do. I assume that it had to do with fear. I was afraid too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But fear of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fear of bombing, attacks, conflicts with terrorists, that's the fear we had, that we would be bombed and that the terrorists would attack us. My policemen had that fear. At that time I wish I could have left the area, going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Ms. Kravetz is asking you this question because the people initially weren't leaving the area, they were all congregating together in the area most likely to be bombed. Why were they doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, unless it was part of some kind of a plan or agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz. I may have misinterpreted your question, so please do not feel confined because of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, it doesn't make sense, does it, that if these people who arrived in the centre of Pec that day feared the NATO bombing they would have left the security of their home and gone out and exposed themselves in the open. That doesn't make sense, does it, that the reason for them gathering there would have been fear of being bombed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, it makes sense to me, I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But by doing so, weren't they more -- weren't they exposing themselves to NATO bombs by gathering in the thousands in the open in the centre of a town? Why would people leave the security of their homes and head out to the road if what they're fearing is that NATO will bomb their home? Why would they do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I also had the impression that we were safer if we were in a crowd, if there was a mass of us, that then we wouldn't be bombed by anyone. I was sure that they wouldn't bomb our buildings that were in town, that everyone would try to avoid a large number of civilian casualties. Believe me, in that situation I would have preferred going along with these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what happened to these people? I mean they gathered there and where did they go later?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Some went towards Djakovica, others went towards Montenegro through Kula, yet others went towards Mitrovica. So they went in those directions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was -- were -- was the police monitoring the departure of these people from the town of Pec when they left in these different directions? Was this something that was monitored by the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: We had a certain number of patrols at key points where there could be bottlenecks. If that's what you mean, then the police was following this and they were providing information if there were some roads that were totally crowded. I had information that the road towards Kula, the road in the mountains, was jammed. At the check-point at Savine Vode people in vehicles were checked. I went to that check-point. I asked for the checks to be made simpler, to keep vehicles there for as short as possible, to do things just by looking at vehicles. Further on some cars broke down which impeded traffic further. So I asked patrols if they could go out there and regulate traffic there. So I'd rather say that we were checking the roads themselves than movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, what roughly was the ethnic division in Pec between Albanians and non-Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just had assessments or estimates. For a long period of time there hadn't been a census, so we really had no idea how many Albanians there were there. However, if we are to speak in terms of estimates we could say that the ratio was 80:20 or 75:25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And would the same ratio apply in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as Istok and Klina are concerned, that would be around it roughly. Again, I'm only talking about estimates, our estimate of the Albanian population figures. They didn't want to take part in a census, they refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did the bulk of -- of the 20 per cent, what sort of proportion were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One-third. That was the ratio roughly, 7, 8, 9. When I came to Pec the information I got was that there was 7 per cent Montenegrins, 8 per cent Serbs, and 9 per cent Muslims, that's what people told me then, and that's how I remembered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware at all of groups of Serbs gathering in the centre of Pec for safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you went to a check-point where there was problems with the traffic and you asked for the traffic to be made or the crossing of the check-point to be facilitated. Was this a border check-point that you went to where there were problems with the circulation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a border check-point. It was a check-point along one of the roads. At the time, there was no border in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who was manning that check-point?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: At that check-point there were members of the traffic police, members of the general police force, and some members from the crime police. There was a permanent check-point that had existed for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you tell us in your statement that the columns of refugees crossed the border into Montenegro, Macedonia, and Albania by car and on foot. Were these columns of refugees that were heading in these directions escorted by men of your SUP, Pec SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
