utterances.text: No. Excuse me, I don't know whether I noted that they crossed the border. I may have wanted to say they were leaving towards. I don't know what exactly the phrase is in the statement. In any case, they were not escorted by any members of the Pec SUP or the traffic police from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Once a state of war was declared, were there -- was there any procedure in place that allowed the police to requisition privately owned vehicle or company-owned vehicles for the use of the police? Was there any procedure in place for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No. The police could seize something that had been used in the commission of a crime, and in that case they were supposed to issue a receipt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that the -- for the VJ there was a procedure which entitles the owner to receive a receipt and later compensation when his vehicle was seized. You're telling us the police could not seize any private vehicles following a similar procedure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No. I am familiar with that part by chance. In order for us to register a vehicle, we asked for confirmation that it had been registered with the police in case it should be commandeered. I think that's what it was about. I don't know that the police had such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we are having a problem with the transcript. I think on two places. The first is the witness has answered -- let me just find out - 18, 2, not only commission of a crime but also as a result of a crime, so both of it. And the second thing is in 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That one I don't understand before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Something can be seized because it's been used in the commission of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you would naturally expect the police to seize something that was the proceeds of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That -- well, that is what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to be as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the second thing is in 18, 7, 8, 9, the witness was talking about the mobilisation, which is, in fact, the material obligation which we heard evidence about that, and it is not in the transcript. I mean, it was translated not properly I think. The essence of the witness's answer was that the police asked the owners of the vehicles when they wanted to renew their registration if they have registered their vehicle with the army in case of mobilisation of the vehicle. And that is what he was actually talking about there about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the mistake in line 9 is a reference to the police instead of the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, so other -- other than those circumstances that you have described when the police is authorised to seize a vehicle and that was in the commission of a crime and what's recently been clarified what was the other situation, if the police seizes a vehicle belonging to a private individual, that requisition would be illegal; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Completely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, we have heard testimony here in this court of persons who were in the centre of Pec on 27th March, these are Kosovo Albanians, and they told this Chamber that the reason they had gathered there was because they had been forced out of their homes by Serb forces at gunpoint and ordered to gather in the centre of town. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We also heard evidence that buses were organized for these persons who were there, these Kosovo Albanians who were there in Pec, to take them to the border. Are you aware of that taking place on that day in Pec town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The bus traffic was in order, if I understood you correctly. I guess you wanted to know whether there were buses organized to transport them. I'm telling you that the bus traffic was functioning without any particular problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The persons who testified here told us that the police had organized buses to get the Albanian population out of the town and to transport them to the border.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You did not see this taking place while you were there in Pec town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, not in a single case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These officers that were from your department that were there that you say these 30 officers, they were armed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that there were also Serb soldiers in the centre of town and local armed civilians who were forcing the population who had been forced to gather there out of the town, directing the population out of the town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a part of this question was already answered. It was said that there was no presence of the army in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The context is important and the question is admissible in its context, so please continue with it, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And one more thing, I'm sorry, Your Honour, but the witness explained where his police officers were on the check-points, not in the centre of the town 30 police officers. He described -- maybe it's not understandable for us who do not know that town, but I think that he tried to explain that those 30 were not in the centre of the town but in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question that's being the asked. The question is based on evidence that we've heard already in the case at an earlier stage. So I think you should pose the question again, Ms. Kravetz, but there's no reason why it should be altered in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that in addition to your police officers there were also Serb soldiers in the centre of town and local armed civilians who were forcing the population that had gathered there out of the town, they were directing this population out of the town and towards the border?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: When I was there, there were none. I don't have any knowledge pertaining to other periods of time. When I was in the centre of town there were no army members. I didn't see a single armed civilian either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're telling us you did not see anyone forcing the civilians who had gathered there to head to the border towards -- in the direction of the border with Montenegro, Albania. Is that really your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you did not see Serb forces loading civilians onto trucks, civilians that had gathered there, and transporting them out of the town?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. I will move on then from that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That last question referred to trucks, is that what you meant to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I had asked about buses and now I was asking about trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, during your testimony today you spoke about an order that you received from the minister of interior to organize documentation when you were based in Kragujevac. Do you recall you spoke at length about this documentation and the compilation of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when that took place, when you worked on this project that you described to organize the documentation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: It was in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had left the SUP of Pec municipality in June of 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said that at the time you took with you, you and your fellow police officers, took with you the documents that were in the archives of the SUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I did not, but some policemen did. That was before I left the area. The fact is that it was transported from SUP Pec and other organizational units to, for example, Kragujevac and some other places in different parts of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When were these documents transported out of the SUP of Pec municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Around those days when the police was withdrawing, or rather, leaving the territory of the SUP, I mean June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many members of the Pec SUP relocated to Kragujevac, approximately if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't arrive in Kragujevac around that time. I arrived in Kragujevac later because I remained in the area of Pec. When I arrived there the situation was not orderly because we didn't know where the police of SUP Pec were. There was no accommodation that had been secured for them. They were finding accommodation whichever way they could. They were also trying to find places for their families to stay, to go on with their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When did you arrive to Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I arrived to Kragujevac on the 26th of June or the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You're talking -- this is 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you remained there until 2002, when you were tasked with this project of organizing the documentation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, and later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what were the specific instructions you received from the minister of interior regarding this project that you embarked on, this project was it dealing with the organization of the documentation of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: They were in written form.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what were the instructions you had received? What were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were strict prerequisites that case files be gathered and sorted out the way I have described. First we had to gather all the case files and to compile -- complete individual files, then a list had to be drawn up as well as statistical tables. And based on that a joint document was supposed to contain all of the information so as to be able to navigate through it more easily. It was strictly prescribed how things were to be designated, how certain security-related events will be marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, you have explained all that earlier in your testimony. Do you know the reasons why three years after or approximately three years after you had moved, relocated, your SUP to Kragujevac you were requested to organize the documentation of the SUP? Why was this done three years after you had moved there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I'm afraid -- well, I don't know, but I'm a bit afraid or hesitant to express my view since you may find it not particularly serious or founded. My first impression was that someone was preparing a Ph.D. thesis. It was organized in a way of a research of significant scope. That was my first impression once we started working on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, but was -- but didn't you say that the order that you got was coming from the ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would it be normal procedure for the ministry in Belgrade to send you an order of this kind if the purpose of gathering this and organizing this documentation was for the purposes of academic research?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. You asked me why it was being done, and I told you what my impression was at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Weren't you the person who was put in charge of this project?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: In the part pertaining to Pec, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And weren't the reports pertaining to Pec signed by you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you're saying you have no idea why you received these instructions to put this material together?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I can only assume. We at the Ministry of the Interior carry out our tasks as received. It is not up to me to assess why I had been given a task; it is up to me to implement it. There is only a single case in which I do not have to carry it out if it is against the law. All other tasks I implement, without going into it whether I like it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Wasn't the purpose of preparing these reports based on your documentation to assist Mr. Milosevic who was at trial here before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Didn't you -- didn't --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: If you're asking me for my opinion, I can share it with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm asking you what you know based on your experience at the time and information you had.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Didn't you include specific references to the indictment against Mr. Milosevic in some of these reports?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why did you do that if the purpose wasn't to assist the defence of Mr. Milosevic before this Tribunal? Why would you include references to the indictment against him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Because it was probably stipulated in the task. If it was indeed mentioned, if there are references, then that must have been our working task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You're saying it was probably stipulated, you do not recall why this was done, these reports that you yourself signed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you do not recall why in these reports that you signed, you included references to the Milosevic indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: It is certain that we did not make it up. For sure I didn't mention the indictment against Mr. Milosevic because I wanted to. It is most likely that there was a request to which we were supposed to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say that you were specifically instructed in this order you received from the ministry to include these references in the reports that you were compiling?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily have to be that way. It may have been mentioned in one of the documents asking us to respond to this and that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Respond to this and that. What do you mean by that? When you say to respond to this and that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I mean if we mentioned something in relation to the indictment there must have been a request for us to provide information or provide indications of information that may have to do with the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was it, Mr. Paponjak, that you became the chief of the SUP Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: In July 1999. July. I was appointed acting chief I think on the 12th of June, and in July a decision was released on my appointment as chief of the Pec SUP. I think the decision was passed by the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What happened to your predecessor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: He was then assigned to other duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Duties as a police officer, and I'm afraid I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, with the Pec SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he demoted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: In terms of rank, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the rumour?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No one shared any with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Borislav Vlahovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is he now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. I retired late in 2004, and I haven't really been in touch since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he still in the police in 2004?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you have absolutely no suspicion of why he was demoted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, I can't say I spent any time considering that. Truth to tell, my own appointment sort of took me aback. I expected that after everything that had happened I would be taking some time off, some time to rest a little. And then this appointment came which surprised me. To be perfectly honest, I can't say that I was really looking forward to this appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that your predecessor was being demoted, you weren't even concerned to find out why just in case the problem might end up in your -- or on your plate?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Anyone who knows me knows that I tend not to ask too many questions about what's going on unless it concerns me directly. I spent a long time working in the police, and this is a type of behaviour that I picked up along the way; other than that, I also happen to be that kind of person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a short one, Your Honour. Further Re-examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon yet again, Mr. Paponjak. Several questions from me. First of all, there's a certain amount of confusion created by this. Why do you not know the regular forces of the VJ. Are those soldiers doing their regular military term or just members of units of the VJ from the Pec area or they came from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I know that there were those that came from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I need. We talked about weapons being seized -- vehicles being seized. Can police seize a vehicle that had been involved in the commission of a crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can the police seize a vehicle that was used in order to commit a crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they are under an obligation to do just that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Edison Zatriqi, who was a haulier from Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, he was a haulier from Pec, that being the reason I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know where he kept his buses in early March 1999, or rather, let me ask you something else to begin with, it's something that I think we have discussed already. The garage where police vehicles were kept, did that garage burn down at one point?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you now remember where the Zatriqi Edison buses were parked at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they were parked nearby, just next to that workshop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when the garage burned down did the police suffer any damage as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did that affect the way in which police vehicles were maintained?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. The owner of that garage, which ethnic group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: He was an ethnic Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We talked about this. You tried to say but somehow you didn't make it. Tell us your opinion, your opinion, on why these reports were compiled. What did you tell me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: My impression was they were compiled in order to assist this Tribunal with its work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just another question from me. You, what about you in the Pec SUP, did you have green and blue APCs positioned at junctions, traffic junctions, where police were waving people on and sending them to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have any APCs at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Paponjak.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No, my intention is to at least make sure that I myself remain protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, when was damage done to Zatriqi's buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right at the beginning of the air-strikes, the 24th, possibly the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many buses did he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They burned down along with a workshop or a garage next to which they were parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, we're not getting transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on LiveNote if you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were these buses destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, burned down to the ground. I remember that he had a double-decker as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it that his buses did not provide the normal service of buses in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were being used until such time as they burned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you told us that the buses were running as usual in March, 27th and 28th ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they ran to schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it would have been better to phrase the question this way. What were his buses normally used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The buses were used to get passengers, for example, from Pec to Belgrade. He drove some of my friends and that's why I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When being used that way, was it a regular-service bus that would travel at a particular time between Pec and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That completes your evidence, Mr. Paponjak. Thank you for assisting us with your evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just -- Mr. Paponjak, can we just clarify one thing arising from your questions. We should see how much these four buses affected normal transportation even if destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you wish to ask that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Please return, Mr. Paponjak. I was premature in thinking that your evidence was complete. Mr. Lukic wants to ask some more questions. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, you were asked about those four buses that burned down?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there a public, state-owned transportation company in Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many inhabitants in Pec roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Between 50.000 and 70.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I know you don't like figures, I have come to realize that while working with you, how many buses were there regularly operating throughout the Pec area, a ballpark figure, do your best, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The socially owned company was poorly equipped. They didn't really have good buses or safe buses. They had a total of about 20. The problem was resolved through the service of private hauliers who had their own private pools of vehicles. That's why I knew Mr. Zatriqi because I became interested when I saw the buses, I wanted to know who they belonged to, and I was told at the time that they belonged to him and he had very good buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many such private hauliers in the general whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: A total of maybe about six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the four buses that you mentioned, the ones that burned down, did that kind of damage really reduce the traffic potential in the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, to some extent. It was more difficult at that point in time to travel to Belgrade, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything arise for you, Ms. Kravetz? That now completes your evidence, Mr. Paponjak. You may this time leave without fear of further detention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm in even a worse position than the last week. What I can propose -- we don't have any more witnesses for the 15 minutes left, and we may have that Status Conference tomorrow morning instead of afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was suggested to you last week that this situation would arise this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to dealt with it but we were informed only people can come on Wednesday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That means someone's coming tonight. Now, if we have the hearing first thing tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now nobody came, we said no, because we wouldn't have enough time to prepare the witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why? Maybe that's one of the problems we have in this Tribunal, that far too much time is spent on preparing witnesses rather than getting them into court and having them examined. A witness who came tonight could surely be seen if we delayed the start of his evidence while we have the hearing in the morning, then his evidence could have begun in the second session or later. Where's the difficulty with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we don't show enough documents to our witnesses, they cannot cope with our examination at all. We really have to go through many of documents, even lately when we were too overburdened with the witnesses, we -- you could hear that we didn't show them some crucial evidence and we really didn't have time to cover everything. Then they have problem with you because they cannot answer some questions and they seemed unreliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the dead-line for the written filing on the issue of -- that we're going to look at tomorrow on the impact of the statement of accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was this afternoon, Your Honour, and it has been filed already, and it is already on the docket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've known, Mr. Lukic, all along what action we're likely to take in a situation like this. In the case of the Prosecution it was of no effect because they did not use all their time; in your case it may well be of some effect if you use all your time as all the indications suggest. We'll make a final decision when the time comes, but you should have regard to the fact that the time lost tomorrow, at least to the extent of one half --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll try to organize ourselves during this break and to -- we'll try to organize ourselves during this break and to use our time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And as an indication I think to everyone of the basis on which you might wish to work, between now and the break that we will have on the 25th of April there are I think 17 days, sitting days in April. And on the face of it, that should be enough to deal with the remaining evidence for your case and the expert evidence for all accused. So you should proceed on the basis that there is a distinct possibility of all these witnesses being required during that period. So far as tomorrow is concerned, if it's convenient to everyone else, then we can have the hearing at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Ms. Kravetz, that a problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, that's fine by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, in the absence of any dissent, we will rise now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24
